claim: In the capability theory that underlies economic complexity, SPECIFIC LABOUR SKILLS are one of the non-tradable capabilities that make a country productive; income differences are attributed to the diversity of locally available capabilities.
what_is_established_or_contested: This is the DEFINITIONAL core of the ECI framework (not an empirical estimate). It treats skills/education as ONE input among many non-tradable capabilities (property rights, regulation, infrastructure, labour skills) and is compatible with education contributing to complexity, but does not test it.
direction_or_sign: + (capacity interpretation: skills are one of the capabilities)
reported_magnitude_verbatim: "some of the individual activities ... cannot be imported, such as property rights, regulation, infrastructure, specific labor skills, etc., and so countries need to have them locally available in order to produce. Hence, the productivity of a country resides in the diversity of its available non-tradable capabilities"
source_title: The building blocks of economic complexity
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 106(26):10570-10575
notes: p.2 of the PNAS paper (text downloaded and read 2026-11-20). This is the textual basis of the user's education->complexity hypothesis, but it is a THEORY of capabilities, not an estimate of education's effect.

claim: The authors explicitly argue that AGGREGATE human capital measured as YEARS OF SCHOOLING is an inadequate proxy for capabilities, and that the search for detailed capabilities (not aggregate schooling) is what development strategy needs.
what_is_established_or_contested: ESTABLISHED as the authors' own stated position: aggregate human-capital measures (years of schooling) were hoped to guide policy but cannot capture capabilities. This DIRECTLY supports the programme's flow-vs-stock finding and warns against using years-of-schooling as the education->complexity regressor.
direction_or_sign: schooling-years is a weak/inadequate proxy for capabilities (not a sign claim about a coefficient)
reported_magnitude_verbatim: "Development economics has tended to disregard the search for detailed capabilities and their patterns of complementarity, hoping that aggregate measures of physical capital (e.g., measured in dollars) or human capital (e.g., measured in years of schooling) would provide enough guidance for policy."
source_title: The building blocks of economic complexity
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 106(26):10570-10575
notes: p.14-15 (concluding discussion). Direct textual warrant for the programme's caution that years-of-schooling is the wrong education variable for a complexity outcome.

claim: Country complexity is only WEAKLY correlated with years of schooling (R = 0.13 in 2006) and rule of law (R = 0.22): ECI is not reducible to human capital, and complexity measures predict growth robustly even so.
what_is_established_or_contested: ESTABLISHED (the authors' own computed correlations): complexity is a distinct object from schooling. Implication: a strong education->complexity coefficient should NOT be expected mechanically, and an observed ECI-schooling correlation is informative rather than tautological.
reported_magnitude_verbatim: "they seem to be different from variables such as years of schooling or rule of law, as the correlation between our measures of country complexity and these two variables is low (R is 0.13 and 0.22 respectively for 2006)."
source_title: The network structure of economic output
notes: p.29 of the paper. This is the single most directly relevant caution for the programme's education->ECI matrix: the correlation is weak in the authors' own data, so a positive finding is not trivial and a null is not surprising.

claim: Growth cannot be explained as the accumulation of aggregate factors such as physical or human capital; something affecting the productivity of activities (capabilities/complexity) is needed.
what_is_established_or_contested: ESTABLISHED as the framework's motivation; this is the growth-theory statement that human-capital accumulation alone is insufficient, which motivates treating complexity as the outcome rather than growth.
reported_magnitude_verbatim: "growth cannot be explained as the consequence of the accumulation of aggregate factors such as physical or human capital, but that something else is at stake, something that affects the productivity of economic activities."
source_title: The network structure of economic output
notes: p.2 (introduction). Supports the user's framing that ECI/complexity, not GDP growth, is the right outcome for the education question.

claim: Trade/technology complexity coefficients REMAIN SIGNIFICANT when the log of human capital (years of education) is included in cross-country growth regressions: complexity adds predictive power BEYOND human capital.
what_is_established_or_contested: ESTABLISHED for the authors' sample: complexity is not merely human capital and carries independent information. Note the direction: this is complexity->growth conditional on human capital, NOT education->complexity.
reported_magnitude_verbatim: "the coefficients of the trade and technology ECI remain significant even when including the log of population and the log of human capital"
source_authors: Stojkoski, Viktor; Koch, Philipp; Hidalgo, Cesar A.
source_title: Multidimensional economic complexity and inclusive green growth
notes: p.6 (results). Useful for the reverse question (complexity beyond human capital) and for the programme's warning that ECI and schooling measure different things.
